title: Copula Complement
definition: The argument of a [term:copula] that specifies what the [term:subject] is, does, or is like — distinct from the [term:predicate] itself. In Dixon's framework, the copula verb is the predicate (it carries tense and links the subject to its complement); the complement is an argument, not a predicate. In 'The river is wide', the copula 'is' is the predicate; 'wide' is the copula complement (CC) — an argument of that predicate alongside the copula subject 'the river'. This is a critical grammatical distinction: calling 'wide' a 'nominal predicate' (a common error Dixon argues against) misidentifies the grammatical relation. In languages without a copula, an NP or adjective may directly head an intransitive predicate — this is a different construction, not the same as copula complement function.

examples.notes: Dixon (§11.1): 'is' is the predicate (carries tense, takes two arguments). 'wide' is copula complement (CC) — an argument of the predicate, not itself a predicate. Compare: 'the river widens' where widen is the intransitive predicate directly.

examples.translation: The river widens below the waterfall. (intransitive predicate — no copula)
examples.notes: Contrast: 'widen' is a derived intransitive verb heading the predicate directly. There is no copula and no copula complement. 'widen' = adjective 'wide' + suffix -en. 'narrow' lacks -en so the parallel is 'the river narrows' (intransitive predicate) vs. 'the river is narrow' (copula + CC).
